archetype.name: Game Manager (veteran backup)
archetype.definition: A 33-year-old undrafted spot starter who wins, when he wins, by staying on schedule with short, low-risk throws and avoiding sacks, not by pushing the ball or creating outside structure.

report.headline: Two disastrous cameos; the career says replacement-level backup, not this bad
report.take:
Cooper Rush is the Falcons' third quarterback, listed QB3 as of Oct. 19, and his 2026 season is two September appearances: a Week 1 start at Pittsburgh and 58% of the snaps in a 3-34 Week 2 home loss to Carolina after Tua Tagovailoa started. Michael Penix Jr. has started every game since Week 3. So this is a 46-dropback sample, and it reads as one. The numbers are about as bad as a qualifier can post: -0.635 EPA per dropback (46th of 47), a 10.3% interception rate (last), a -13.61 CPOE and a bad-throw rate of 23.1%, last among charted passers.

What drove it is narrow and identifiable. On throws under 10 air yards he was merely below average, near neutral on the 0-9 range with a 50% success rate. Once he tried to work the 10-19 window, everything broke: 7 attempts, 3 interceptions, -12.2 EPA. Add a fourth-quarter, one-score sequence that produced an interception and a sack for -10.8 EPA, and two drives explain most of the damage. His intended air yards (5.34) and aggressiveness (7.69%) show he was playing small even before the turnovers.

The career separates the real from the noise. Rush has never been accurate. His CPOE has been negative every season, and 2022 and 2024 ranked in the bottom tier. That part is who he is, though this year's figure is far deeper than even last season's -1.9. What he has always done is avoid sacks under pressure: his pressure-to-sack rate ranked 4th, 11th and 2nd in his three charted seasons. This year's 62.5% is the opposite, and it came behind a line that ranks 2nd in hit rate allowed. That points to a small-sample blip, not a collapsed skill. The same goes for the interception rate. His career rates are bad but nowhere near one pick per ten throws.

Where this goes: probably nowhere on the field. As QB3 behind an established starter, Rush only matters if two quarterbacks go down. If that happens, expect the 2024 version, a check-down passer living around 6 yards an attempt who keeps a run-leaning offense afloat for a game or two, rather than the September turnover machine.

strengths.title: Historic sack avoidance under pressure
strengths.body: Across 2022, 2024 and 2025 Rush ranked near the top of the league at not taking sacks when pressured, a product of quick decisions and a willingness to throw it away or check it down. This season's 62.5% conversion of pressures into sacks contradicts three years of evidence on a handful of pressures. With a line ranked 2nd in hit rate allowed, the career trait is the better bet if he plays again.

strengths.title: Short game stays on schedule
strengths.body: Inside 10 air yards he completed 63.3% with half his 0-9 throws producing positive EPA, roughly break-even football. Throws to the left side (+0.482 EPA, 83.3% completions) and to Drake London were the only productive slices. It is a thin foundation, but it is the version of Rush a run-first offense can survive.

concerns.title: Intermediate throws turned into turnovers
concerns.body: Three of his four interceptions came on just 7 attempts in the 10-19 yard range, and his 10-plus throws as a group cost -1.462 EPA each with a third completed. Rush has never had the arm talent or anticipation to live there, which is why his aDOT has always been modest. The rate will cool with volume, but the limitation behind it is real.

concerns.title: Accuracy far below even his norm
concerns.body: A -13.61 CPOE and a bad-throw rate ranked last are worse than any season on his record. They are also 11.7 points of CPOE below last year. Some of it is sample and the chaos of a blowout relief appearance; his Week 2 bad-throw rate was 29.4%. But his career CPOE has always been negative, so the realistic rebound is to below average, not to average.

concerns.title: Can't convert third-and-long
concerns.body: He converted 15.4% of third downs at an average of 8.5 yards to go, taking three sacks on 13 plays. A checkdown passer facing long yardage lacks the tools to move the sticks, and his -5.03 air yards to sticks shows he was throwing well short of them. In this offense, a backup who can't extend drives hands the ball back quickly.

trend.note: Week 1 at Pittsburgh was poor but functional (143 yards, a TD, -15.8 EPA); Week 2's relief stint against Carolina was worse in accuracy, bad throws and turnovers. He hasn't taken a meaningful snap since and slid to QB3 behind Penix.

nextGame.headline: QB3 unlikely to play; Cincinnati's soft underneath defense cuts both ways
nextGame.body:
Rush is not expected to take snaps against Cincinnati with Penix starting, so this matters only in an emergency. If he were pressed in, the matchup splits along his profile. The Bengals allow +0.177 EPA on short throws (27th) and give up the third-most passing yards to quarterbacks, exactly where a checkdown passer lives. They also post the 2nd-best sack rate, which tests the pressure-to-sack problem that hurt him in September. Cincinnati's offense ranks 5th in EPA and the total sits at 52.5 with Atlanta a 3-point home underdog. A game script that forces passing volume would pull a run-first offense into Rush's weakest mode.

On Atlanta's side, the absences are depth pieces: WR Zachariah Branch (24% of snaps) and RB Brian Robinson Jr. (30%) are out, and WR Beaux Collins and OL Cameron Williams remain on IR without having played. For the Bengals, CB DJ Turner II (95% of snaps) is questionable with an ankle. Losing him would thin a secondary that already gives up yardage underneath. S Kyle Dugger is out, but he is a part-timer.

keyMatchups.title: Short-area throws vs soft underneath coverage
keyMatchups.body: Cincinnati ranks 27th in EPA allowed on short passes. That is the one area where Rush's game was near break-even this season. Any relief appearance would likely lean on Bijan Robinson and quick hitters.

keyMatchups.title: Bengals pass rush vs sack tendency
keyMatchups.body: The Bengals' 8.2% sack rate ranks 2nd, and Rush converted pressure into sacks at a league-worst clip this year. His career says that should normalize, but this is the wrong opponent to bet on it.

keyMatchups.title: Tight ends find room
keyMatchups.body: Cincinnati lets the top tight end score 3.9 PPR over his average (30th) and sees an above-league share of targets go to tight ends. Kyle Pitts was a disaster on Rush's 4 targets, but the matchup invites those throws.

nextGame.watch: Whether Rush is still QB3 on the inactive/active list. Only an injury to the starter puts him in play.

restOfSeason.body:
The likeliest outcome is no meaningful snaps: Penix has started six straight and Rush sits third. If injuries force him into a start, his career profile says to expect a conservative short passer who completes around 60%, averages about 6 yards an attempt and takes few sacks. The September version was worse than that, with an interception every tenth throw, a 62.5% pressure-to-sack rate and a last-ranked bad-throw rate. Those numbers came on too few plays to trust and run against three prior seasons. The inaccuracy and the inability to push the ball past 10 yards are real and permanent; the turnover and sack extremes should regress.

The projections below are per start, if he gets one. Atlanta's run-leaning approach (29th in pass rate over expected) caps his volume, so even a start likely means modest yardage.
swingFactors: Health of the two quarterbacks ahead of him
Whether his career sack avoidance returns
How much the offense leans on the run if he starts

confidence.note: 46 dropbacks across two games, one a blowout relief stint, from a QB3 unlikely to play.
